newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks hammered by inflation worries.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks hammered by inflation worries.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average fell nearly 150 points Friday on signs that underlying inflation was showing some unwanted vitality and as long-term interest rates soared to the highest levels since last July.

The Dow finished with a loss of 148.36 points, or 2.27 percent, at 6,391.69. It was off 134.38 points for the week, its fifth straight down week. The last time the index racked up such a string of declining weeks was in the last quarter of 1991.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,322 to 379 on moderate volume of 440 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
A surprising jump in underlying wholesale prices in March forced investors to recast their outlook for inflation and interest rates.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index fell 0.1 percent in March, but the underlying rate, which excludes often-volatile food and energy costs, rose an unexpected 0.4 precent.
Analysts said that rise, far higher than the 0.1 percent economists had forecast, meant the Federal Reserve was likely to become more aggressive in raising interest rates.

"This increases the odds of a Fed tightening very dramatically in May," said Pierre Ellis, senior international economist at Primark Decision Economics. "A 50-basis point (one-half percentage point) move is definitely on the table and the Fed almost looks behind the curve."

In the inflation-sensitive Treasury bond market, the benchmark 30-year bond fell 21/32, and its yield, which moves in the opposite direction of its price, jumped to 7.17 percent -- the highest since July 8 during the stock market's last big slump -- from 7.11 percent Thursday.
As in July, analysts are again concerned about the implications of a surprisingly strong and persistent pace of economic growth.

"There's a cycle out there and it's accelerating," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "It's looking more and more like a boom to be followed at some time later by a bust."
Regardless of what comes next, the market's recent woes rank as some of the worst it has endured since embarking on its stunning ascent in early 1995.
Since its last record close of 7,085.16 on March 11, the Dow is off 693 points or nearly 9.8 percent, within a whisker of the 10 percent customarily considered to represent a significant correction.
The market's drop for the week was the first time since late 1991 that the average has fallen for five straight weeks.

"The times have changed dramatically," said Yale Hirsch, of the Hirsch Organisation, publisher of the Stock Trader's Almanac. "During the last 13 years, bear markets have tended to be much shorter affairs."

In fact, Hirsch said, stocks ran into only two longer losing streaks since 1984, once that year and again in 1990, after the outbreak of the Persian Gulf War. In each case, the declines lasted six weeks, he said.
Few stocks dodged the selling pressure.
Financial stocks were among the hardest hit, with Chase Manhattan Corp. down 3-7/8 to 90-1/4, Bank of New York Co. off 1-7/8 to 33-7/8 and Citicorp shedding 5-1/4 to 104-7/8.
Technology stocks were also broadly weaker. Intel Corp. tumbled 6-3/4 to 130-1/2, in part on concern about the company's plans to cut microprocessor prices.
Boston Scientific Corp. slid 14-3/8 to 46-1/8 after the company warned its first quarter results would fall short of analysts estimates.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 28.87 points, or 2.34 percent, to 1,206.90.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks lost 20.69 to 737.65. The American Stock Exchange index fell 7.06 to 556.13.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 9.89 to 389.47. The average share was down $1.00.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,059.97, down 178.162 or 2.46 percent.
